Cancer medicines, A to Z

Look up a medicine your care team mentioned, by brand name or generic name. Each entry explains what kind of medicine it is, what it is often used for and how it is usually given.

Combination names you may hear

Many treatments combine medicines and are known by an abbreviation.

ContainsOften used for
R-CHOPRituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin (hydroxydaunorubicin), vincristine (Oncovin) and prednisoneMany B-cell lymphomas
BRBendamustine and rituximabCLL and some lymphomas
FOLFOXFolinic acid (leucovorin), fluorouracil (5-FU) and oxaliplatinColorectal and other digestive cancers
FOLFIRINOXFolinic acid, fluorouracil, irinotecan and oxaliplatinPancreatic cancer
AC-TDoxorubicin (Adriamycin) and cyclophosphamide, followed by a taxane (paclitaxel or docetaxel)Breast cancer
Carboplatin and paclitaxelCarboplatin and paclitaxelOvarian, lung and other cancers
VRdBortezomib (Velcade), lenalidomide (Revlimid) and dexamethasoneMultiple myeloma

Types of treatment, in plain words

Chemotherapy

Medicines that damage fast-growing cells. Common effects include tiredness, nausea, low blood counts (higher infection risk), mouth sores and, with some medicines, hair loss or numbness in hands and feet.

Immunotherapy

Helps your own immune system find and attack cancer. Side effects come from inflammation and can affect skin, gut, lungs, liver or hormone glands — sometimes months later. Report any new symptom.

Targeted therapy

Blocks a specific signal the cancer uses to grow. Side effects depend on the target and may include rash, diarrhea, high blood pressure or changes in blood counts.

Antibody therapy

Lab-made antibodies that attach to a marker on cancer cells, such as rituximab on lymphoma cells. Infusion reactions and infections are the main things your team watches for.

Hormone therapy

Lowers or blocks hormones that some breast and prostate cancers need. Hot flashes, joint aches, tiredness and bone thinning are common.

Supportive care

Medicines that prevent or treat side effects — nausea, low blood counts, bone problems or blood clots — so treatment is safer and easier.

Call your care team right away if you have

  • A temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, or shaking chills
  • Trouble breathing, chest pain or a new cough
  • Bleeding or bruising that won’t stop
  • Vomiting or diarrhea that won’t stop, or you can’t keep fluids down
  • A new rash, swelling, or a reaction during or after an infusion
  • New confusion, severe weakness or severe pain
For a medical emergency, call 911.

Questions to ask about any new medicine

  1. What is this medicine for, and what is the goal — cure, control or comfort?
  2. How and how often will I get it, and for how long?
  3. Which side effects are common, and which ones mean I should call right away?
  4. Can I take my other medicines, vitamins, herbs or supplements with it?
  5. Will it affect my work, driving, fertility, pregnancy or vaccines?
  6. Who do I call after hours, and what number should I use?
